interest: Shows wartime Japanese labor shortages, with frank periodicals debating convict, POW, and Chinese coolie labor despite propaganda.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.504, covering May 1940 through February 1944) documents the United States government's collection and analysis of intelligence concerning Japan's escalating wartime labor crisis and manpower mobilization policies. Originating from diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, inter-agency correspondence, and intelligence sharing with the British Ministry of Economic Warfare, the file traces Japan's acute shortages of skilled workers and technicians from the pre-Pearl Harbor era into the height of the Pacific War. Key topics include the exhaustion of rural agricultural labor reserves, the inflationary distortion of industrial wages versus falling real living standards, the suppression of independent labor unions and political parties by the Home Ministry, and the regime's increasing reliance on compulsory labor registrations, Korean workers, paroled prisoners, prisoners of war, and prospective Chinese laborers. The records also illustrate the administrative mechanics of wartime economic intelligence, showing how raw open-source Japanese periodicals and foreign press reports were gathered in London, Moscow, and Bern, analyzed by the Office of Economic Warfare and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, and preserved across State Department central and divisional files.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on Japan's acute shortage of skilled workers, declining real wages, suppression of labor statistics, and government restrictions on labor politics.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports to the Secretary of State on the deepening labor crisis in Japan caused by military conscription and rapid industrial expansion. He highlights an acute shortage of skilled technicians across Japan, Manchuria, and North China, noting that the drain on agricultural labor has inflated the cost of living while real wages decline. In contrast, certain skilled munitions workers receive lavish wages up to 30 yen per day, creating friction with government efforts toward spiritual mobilization. Grew also notes that the Home Ministry suppressed an attempt by Isoo Abe to form a new labor party, while official secrecy has prevented the publication of all statistical data on labor conditions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4713 from Tokyo on Labor Problems in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram concerning Japan's basic labor policy formulated under a projected ten-year program for regional economic self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a November 1940 Grew telegram on Japan's labor policy for a ten-year Japan-China-Manchukuo self-sufficiency program.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 1175 on Ten-Year Labor Program

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram reporting demands made by Japanese employees on American commercial enterprises in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Indexes an August 1941 Grew telegram on demands by Japanese employees of American firms anticipating business closures.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 1194 on Japanese Employees' Demands on American Firms

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram from Switzerland submitting Japanese employment statistics.
subfiles.summary: Indexes an August 1943 Harrison telegram from Bern reporting Japanese employment statistics.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram 4947 on Japanese Employment Figures

subfiles.about: Ambassador Harriman reports on Soviet newspaper coverage of Tokyo press reports detailing nationwide compulsory labor registration in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 525: Harriman reports from Moscow that Japan ordered mandatory registration of males 12-60 and females 12-40 for a comprehensive labor allocation registry, per the Nippon Times and Asahi.
subfiles.title: Telegram 525 from Moscow on Japanese Labor Registration and Mobilization

subfiles.about: Internal State Department note advising the Far Eastern Division on procedures for retaining incoming copies of letters addressed to other agencies.
subfiles.summary: Meyer of Records tells Far Eastern Affairs it may keep copies of interagency correspondence for its own files.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Retention of Incoming Inter-Agency Copies by Far Eastern Division

subfiles.about: Internal note requesting permission for the Far Eastern Division to retain an attached London letter and Japanese article translations or have them formally indexed.
subfiles.summary: Benninghoff asks Records to let FE keep a London letter and translations, or give the file number if retained.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Requesting File Retention or Indexing of Economic Warfare Letter

subfiles.about: State Department analysis summarizing three translated Japanese articles covering wartime labor mobilization, unpolished rice rationing, and Manchurian industrial results.
subfiles.summary: Benninghoff summarizes three Japanese periodical articles: a February 1943 Japan Review piece on Japan's labor crisis and reliance on Chinese coolies and POWs, an article urging unpolished rice to save 30% of food, and one on Manchuria's first five-year plan, deemed outdated.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Summarizing Japanese Magazine Articles on Labor, Rice, and Manchuria

subfiles.about: Transmittal letter from the Embassy in London sending translations of Japanese economic articles received from the British Ministry of Economic Warfare to the Office of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: Allison in London sends Max Ways three translated Japanese articles from the British Ministry of Economic Warfare, on labor supply, food shortages, and Manchurian economic planning.
subfiles.title: Letter from Allison to Ways Transmitting Japanese Article Translations

subfiles.about: Translation of an article by Yoshiyuki Tomiishi analyzing labor management restructuring, female employment decline, and potential manpower reserves in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Translated Tomiishi article urges a monthly living wage with efficiency incentives, shows Cabinet statistics that female factory employment fell below 1926 levels, discusses using paroled convicts and POWs, identifies Chinese coolies as the best labor source, and urges adequate food, housing, and clothing for workers.
subfiles.title: Summarized Translation of Tomiishi Article on Wartime Labour Supply
